messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Would you consider this mixing?
parts: > hmm. actually, I don't know. How can I find out?

Are you using RStan? If so I use the function

# Count divergences across all chains
count_divergences <- function(fit) {
sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
}

Divergences are really sensitive diagnostics to
problems that could be causing stray chains.

> My next question would have been how I can find out which parameter may be responsible for that. Since the is sampling is not independent (and I think I understand why), I don't know to track down the issue ... I could maybe fix some parameters (one at a time) to good value and see whether this persists ... But maybe there is a better way?

No, fixing parameters won’t help. That just samples from the corresponding
conditional distribution and doesn’t tell you anything about the joint distribution
that we actually care about.

If you don’t have any guesses as to what could be causing problems then
probably your best bet is to suck it up and look at the samples plotting vs
_every_ pair of parameters. It helps to highlight the ones that ended with
a divergence in a different color than the others. You want to look for
“banana" shapes or really any sharp corner that indicates nonlinear
nonidentifiabilities that are preventing efficient sampling or “funnel” shapes
that indicate bad hierarchical structure.
> It is really frustrating, because 3 out of 4 chains usually look good which I thought is a good sign, but I just can't fix this issue..

It should be relieving because you’re not inadvertently publishing a biased
result!
> From what I see its effective sample size is usually smaller that that of my model parameters.

That’s fine. Functions that vary strongly with respect to the sampled parameters
will converge slower than functions that very weakly. For example, constants
have no variation and converge immediately. The log posterior density tends to
vary strongly and hence converge more slowly.

The real worry is whether or not those ESS estimates (remember, they’re just
numerical estimates) are good. Given what you’re seeing in the chains, they’re
probably not.

Dear all,

this maybe a stupid question, but I have been wondering about the following.

Imagine I have some unused parameters, that is, they are defined but not
connected to any model structure. Do these possibly effect the sampling
of a model in the following situations:

a) There is only the definition (no constraints)
b) There is a definition with upper and lower bounds
c) There is a sampling statement and case (a)
d) There is a sampling statement and case (b)

Intuitively I think case (a) and (b) should not do any harm except some
runtime required for initializing and drawing uniform samples. For case
(c) it still might be just some runtime increase. Case (d) might be more
critical, because the sampling statement may generate to-be-rejected
samples. Furthermore, maybe the adaptation process may be affected by
the pure existence of such dangling parameters?

Many thanks in advance!
Jan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Unused parameters
parts:
The point is that you need a properly normalizable
posterior for Stan to work at all. As long as the
posterior's proper, it should only cause inefficiency,
not failure.

If the model doesn't touch the variable, then the
posterior is equal to the prior.

Stan's default prior is uniform over values meeting
the constraints.

So unconstrained, or just constrained above or below
are improper, constrained above and below are proper.
Simplexes and correlation matrices are proper, ordered
vectors and covariance matrices are improper.

You don't need sampling statements, per se, you can use
increment_log_prob.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Would you consider this mixing?
parts:
It means 23 times you ran into arithmetic troubles due to
underflow, overflow, divide by zero, subtracting two infinite
values, etc. You really want that number to be zero.

You can try running with a higher target acceptance rate and
perhaps smaller initial step size. Youc ould start with

control = list(stepsize=0.01, adapt_delta=0.95)

and keep lowering. By reducing the step size (and targeting
higher accept stat does that post warmup), the first-order
approximation of curvature via stepping according to the gradient
is more stable.

Each of those divergences should print a warning. If you're
not seeing those, you should be. And if you can't figure out
how to see them (I don't know RStan well enough to tell you), please
ask a separate question on the list so people will see it's new
and what the subject is.

- Bob

On Wednesday, October 28, 2015 at 6:33:23 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:

> hmm. actually, I don't know. How can I find out?

Are you using RStan?  If so I use the function

# Count divergences across all chains
count_divergences <- function(fit) {
  sampler_params <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
  sum(sapply(sampler_params, function(x) c(x[,'n_divergent__']))[,1])
}

The rstan 2.8.x package will throw a warning if there are any divergent transitions after warmup that says:

"There were 23 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help."

It will then make another warning suggesting that you use the pairs() function. So, looking at the output of get_sampler_params() should only be necessary if you need to know whether a particular chain is misbehaving.

Ben

If all of the parameters are non-identified then NUTS will diverge to infinity
and a warning thrown in warmup.  But if only some of the parameters are
non-identified then NUTS might terminate the trajectories prematurely and
prevent these divergences from occurring.  So we do diagnose it when we
can, but we can’t always.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Would you consider this mixing?
parts:
Yes, roughly the right idea.  Depends on the exact structure
of your model.  And support up to -80 with a hard constraint
and -100 sounds dangerous — your posterior will probably
be heavy tailed at best.

On Oct 29, 2015, at 10:28 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:

Hi Michael,

I have been trying to do so, but not managed so far.

What I thought is:

The parameter (lets call it delta) usually varies between 0 and -80. Due to some theoretical considerations it does not make sense if this parameter goes outside 100 or -100. All my other paras are roughly between 0 and 1 (and for these it works nicely). So I thought I can bring delta in a good range by doing this:

delta[i] <- (mean*200) + e*(sigma* 200)

Then the mean should vary roughly within -0.5 and 5. Since the delta[i] would have the appropirate scale (and not affect the sampling since they are deterministic).

Is this generally the right (or at least a possible) way do approach this?

It did not work when I tried it. But maybe I just had some bug (some constants, initial values, bounds, etc. musst be adjusted as well... maybe I missed one).

Best regards
Jan



On 10/29/2015 11:18 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Yes, yes, yes, normalize all of your groups to have similar responses!

On Oct 29, 2015, at 10:16 PM, Jan Tünnermann <je...@mail.upb.de> wrote:

While this works great for most parameters, one was producing absurdly high (and autocorrelated) samples in the e[i] while the sigma was approaching zero. I guess the reason was that that this parameter is not normalized and lives on a much larger scale that the others for which it works.

parts:
On Thursday, October 29, 2015 at 3:36:53 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
But what happens to the exception messages that caused the divergences?
They'll indicate where things are going wrong for a user.  

Is there a way to do the R-like thing of buffering them so someone
can look at them later.    I don't think they should just be suppressed
and then thrown away altogether.

They are neither suppressed nor thrown away. The currently are collected so that at the end, it should say something like (in the case of stan_demo("inv_wishart"))

The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times after warmup on chain 4
                                                                                                     count
Exception thrown at line 11: inv_wishart_log: LDLT_Factor of random variable is not positive definit     2
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

followed by

Warning messages:
1: There were 53 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta may help.
2: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems

and the whole stderr is saved in one of the randomly-named files without an extension in tempdir().

Ben
